Neural Network Field Guide

PDFfor printPNGlightPNGdark

42 architectures and training schemes, from the perceptron (1958) to diffusion LLMs (2025).

Each diagram draws a network in miniature, from input at the bottom to output at the top. Most circles are neurons; in sequence models a column is a token, a circle its whole vector at one layer. A square is larger: an image patch, a matrix-valued state, a whole network, or an environment. Color and mark both show a cell’s role, so diagrams read without color. Faded parts play little or no role in the step shown. Parts repeated over positions, windows, copies, or passes share weights; layers, experts, encoders, and decoders drawn alike do not. Sections group by a defining trait: wiring, dynamics, training, cost, or purpose. Years and training methods follow landmark papers, not always the first; many can be trained other ways. Select a diagram for its explanation, key, and papers.

What is a neural network?

A network of simple units

A neural network is built from simple . Most take in numbers, multiply each by a , add them up, and pass the sum through a simple . Units are arranged in , and each layer's outputs feed the next, so simple steps stack into a complicated function of the input. A few panels use units that work differently: some measure a distance to a stored point (RBF), and some apply a learned curve to each input (KAN).

An example: the MLP

In this network, three numbers pass up through two of four units to two outputs, along 36 , one weight each. Move the inputs: each unit adds up what arrives, each value scaled by its line's weight, and squashes the sum to between 0 and 1. Thicker lines carry larger weights, and gray ones subtract; brighter units are more active. Training changes only the weights; the wiring stays as drawn. Randomize weights draws a fresh random set, like a network before training. Real networks also learn a , a number added to each unit's sum; the drawings and this demo leave it out.

The MLP uses only four of the symbols below, each first in its list: the input unit, hidden unit, output unit and connection. The rest appear in other panels, for memory, , and more; each panel's key lists the ones it uses.

Every mark and link

Each color and outer mark names a role, and a cell's shape or a small mark inside it names the kind.

Input

Yellow, with a stem below: data entering the network.

  • Input unit. One number, or one token's vector, fed in.
  • Image patch. A square tile of an image, fed in as one vector.
  • Noisy input. Data with noise added, which the network learns to clean up.
  • Random noise. Random numbers drawn fresh each time, which a generator turns into data.
  • Visible unit (in and out). Set by the data, then updated by the network: in Hopfield and Boltzmann machines the same units are both input and output.
  • Masked token. A token hidden from the network, which it must guess. Hollow, since its value is missing.

Hidden

Green and unmarked: work that stays inside.

  • Hidden unit. Adds up what arrives along its lines and applies a nonlinearity.
  • Probabilistic hidden. Turns on at random, with odds set by its inputs; in the VAE, a code sampled from a learned distribution.
  • Capsule (vector output). Outputs a vector: its length says whether a part is present, its direction how it is posed.
  • Router. Scores the experts and sends each token to the best few.

State

Blue, with a ring: something kept from one step to the next.

  • Recurrent unit. Holds a vector it updates at each step from the new input and its last value.
  • Memory cell. A store kept apart from the working state, written and read by the network: the LSTM's cell, the NTM's memory, Modern Hopfield's stored patterns.
  • Matrix-valued state. A state that is a whole matrix rather than a vector, updated at each step.

Mixing

Pink, with a tick each side: a unit that combines values from many positions.

  • Attention. Weighs every other position by how well it matches, then mixes their values in those proportions. In a Transformer it usually stands for a whole block, attention and the feed-forward layer after it (the decoder's block spans its two attention rows).
  • Convolution or pooling. Applies one small filter at every window of its input, or pools a window into one value.

Output

Red, with a stem above: data leaving the network.

  • Output unit. A result: a prediction, a class score, the next token.
  • Reconstruction of input. The network's attempt to rebuild its own input.
  • Velocity. Which way, and how fast, to move a noisy sample toward real data.

Whole systems

Gray: a whole network as one box.

  • A whole network. Any architecture: an expert, a generator, a denoiser. Panels that show a way of training draw networks this way, since any can fill the role.
  • Environment. The world an agent acts in, outside the network: it takes an action and returns the next state and a reward.

Links

Every line is drawn at one weight; only the dash, the arrowhead or the path differs.

  • Connection. One weight between single units: the value below is scaled by it on the way up. Between whole vectors it is a matrix of weights.
  • Skip connection. Carries a layer's input around it, to be added to its output or joined to a later layer.
  • Data passed on or fed back. Data carried one way: a state to the next step, a message to a neighbor, or, bent around the side, an output fed back in to run the network again.
  • Gate, acting at the dot. A learned signal that sets how much passes along the arrow it meets, at the dot.
  • Similarity score. A weight computed from the input by how well two things match, as in every attention read (what passes still goes through learned weights shared by every line), or the match score itself, as in a similarity.
  • Learnable function. A small learned function in place of a single weight.

Learning means adjusting weights

A network starts with random weights. Training shows it examples, scores how wrong its output is with a (the objective), and nudges every weight to make that score better; works out which way each weight should move. Over many examples, the weights come to encode the task. Most panels here learn this way; a few use local rules instead, such as Hopfield's rule and the Kohonen map's rule.

Architectures differ in wiring

What sets most designs apart is which units connect. connect every unit to every unit in the next layer; connect small and reuse the same weights across them; networks carry a state from one step to the next; attention lets each weigh every other by its content.

Inside a Transformer block

A Transformer stacks one kind of , run the same way at every position. Here one position goes through it: attention reads from it and the positions before it (in an , from all of them); then a small MLP, the , works on that position alone, widening its (to four units here, often four times its size) and narrowing it back. Around each step a adds the step's input to its output, and the sum is (most recent models normalize before each step instead). The panels usually draw all of this as one pink attention cell (the Transformer's decoder spreads its block over two attention rows), and leave out position: the original Transformer adds it to each once, before the first block, while most recent models build it into attention in every block (rotary , RoPE).

Training schemes differ in the goal

The same network can be trained toward different goals: to predict labels, the next word, or a hidden one, or to generate new data, as GANs and do. Panels that show a way of training draw the networks inside as gray boxes, since any network can fill them.

Reading a diagram

Data flows from the inputs at the bottom to the outputs at the top. Each circle is a unit (in sequence models, a whole token's vector), each line a connection (one weight in the MLP), and a cell's color and mark show its role, as the key explains. The diagrams show how parts connect, not complete implementations: normalization, most residual paths and positional information are left out. Select any diagram for its explanation, how it is trained, and where it came from. Step through lights each unit once everything it reads has lit, so stacked layers move along a sequence as a diagonal wave.

Basics

Activation

A unit's output value for a given input: its weighted sum after the activation function.

The activations of a layer together are its representation of the input.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Activation function

The function a unit applies to its weighted sum, such as ReLU (keep positive values, zero out the rest) or a sigmoid (squash any number into 0 to 1).

Without one, any stack of layers would collapse into a single linear map, however deep. KAN learns its functions instead of fixing them.

Used in: Nearly every network here; KAN learns its functions instead of fixing them.

Source: Nair & Hinton 2010; Glorot, Bordes & Bengio 2011

Bias

A number a unit adds to its weighted sum, learned like a weight.

It sets how easily the unit responds, so it can fire even when its inputs are all zero.

Used in: Nearly every network here.

Source:

Class

One of the categories a classifier sorts inputs into, such as cat or dog, or the digits 0 to 9.

A classifier usually gives one output per class, turned into probabilities by a softmax.

Used in: , , , , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Deep learning

Machine learning with networks of many layers, each finding features built from those of the layer below.

It took off in the late 2000s and early 2010s, once more data, faster hardware, and better training methods made deep networks practical; most networks here from the DBN on are deep.

Used in: Nearly every network here; the perceptron, the Hopfield network, and the Kohonen map are shallow.

Source: LeCun, Bengio & Hinton 2015

Dense and sparse

A dense (fully connected) layer links every unit to every unit of the layer before.

Sparse means few: a sparse code has only a few units active at once, as in a sparse autoencoder, and a sparse mixture of experts runs only a few experts per token.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Embedding

A learned vector that stands for an item, such as a token, an image, or a sentence.

Training places similar items near each other, so distance in the space means something.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source: Bengio et al. 2003; Mikolov et al. 2013

Feature

A property of the input that a unit responds to, such as an edge, a texture, or a word's tense.

Early layers find simple features and later ones combine them; a convolution's output, one feature measured at every position, is a feature map.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Hidden layer

A layer between the input and the output, whose values no one sets or reads directly.

Hidden layers let a network build its own features, which is what lets it learn more than a straight-line boundary.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source:

Input and output

The input is the data a network is given, such as an image's pixels or a sentence's tokens; the output is what it produces, such as a label, the next token, or an image.

The guide marks them with stems: below an input, above an output.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Layer

A row of units that read the same inputs and work side by side.

A network's depth is its number of layers; in the guide each row of cells is one.

Used in: Every network here.

Source:

Link

A line between two cells in the guide's diagrams.

Its style says what it carries: a plain line a learned weight, dashed a weight set by similarity, dotted a gate, an arrow data passed on, a wavy line a learned function. The key lists them.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Parameters

A network's learned numbers: its weights and biases.

A mixture of experts can have many parameters but use only a few experts per token, so its active parameters, the ones each token runs through, are far fewer.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016;

Patch

One of the small squares an image is cut into, flattened into a vector and treated as a token.

ViT reads a 224-by-224 image as 196 patches of 16 by 16 pixels.

Used in: ,

Source:

ReLU

Rectified linear unit: the activation function that passes a positive sum unchanged and turns a negative one to zero.

Cheap, and easy to train through many layers, it became the default in deep networks in the early 2010s.

Used in: , , ,

Source: Nair & Hinton 2010; Glorot, Bordes & Bengio 2011

Softmax

A function that turns a list of scores into weights that are positive and add up to 1, giving the largest scores most of the weight.

Attention uses it to weigh positions, a language model to turn scores into the next token's probabilities.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Bridle 1989

Target

The output training wants for an input: the right label, the actual next token, or the direction a flow should move.

The loss measures how far the output is from it.

Used in: , , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Token

One item of a sequence as a model reads it: a word or part of a word, an image patch, a sound sample.

Each becomes a vector before the network sees it.

Used in: , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch 2016

Unit

The basic element of a network, also called a neuron: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the sum through an activation function.

The guide draws one as a circle.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: McCulloch & Pitts 1943;

Vector

An ordered list of numbers, such as a unit's weights or a token's embedding: a point, or a direction, in a space with one axis per number.

Most of what flows through a network is vectors.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Weight

A number on a connection that scales whatever passes along it.

Training adjusts the weights; they are what a network learns. Most lines in the guide stand for one.

Used in: Every network here.

Source:

XOR

Exclusive or: true when exactly one of two inputs is on.

Its true and false cases can't be split by one straight line, so a perceptron can't learn it, while a network with a hidden layer can; Minsky and Papert's 1969 analysis of such limits is often blamed for slowing the field for years.

Used in: ,

Source: Minsky & Papert 1969;

Operations

Associative memory

A memory recalled by content rather than address: given part of a stored pattern, or a noisy copy, it returns the whole.

Its capacity is how many patterns it can store before recall breaks down.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Attention

A way for each position in a sequence to gather what it needs from the others.

Each position asks a question, its query, of every position it can see; each answers with a key, and how well the two match decides how much of that position's value it takes. So the weights are set by the input itself, unlike a layer's learned weights, which is why the guide draws them dashed. Self-attention reads the same sequence; cross-attention reads another, such as the source sentence in translation. A layer runs several heads at once, each matching on something different.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Bidirectional

Reading a sequence both ways, so each position sees what comes after it as well as before.

Encoders that read a whole input at once are bidirectional; a model that generates one token at a time can't be, since what comes after doesn't exist yet.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Block

A small group of layers repeated to build a deep network, such as a Transformer's attention and feed-forward layers with their residual connections.

Stacking the same block many times is how most deep networks are made; the primer opens one.

Used in: , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Bottleneck

The narrowest layer of a network that squeezes its input and widens it again, which forces it to keep only what matters.

In an autoencoder the bottleneck is the code; in U-Net it is the coarsest scale, with skip connections carrying the fine detail around it.

Used in: , ,

Source: ;

Capsule

A group of units whose output is a vector: its length says how likely an entity is present, and its direction describes it, such as its pose.

Capsules pass their outputs on by routing by agreement.

Used in:

Source:

Causal mask

In a model that generates a sequence, each position may read only the ones before it, so in training it cannot see what it is learning to predict.

The guide draws it as lines that only reach back, never forward. WaveNet gets the same effect from causal convolutions, which only look back.

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Channel

One of the stacked maps at each position of a convolutional layer, such as red, green, and blue in an image, or one filter's output deeper in.

A filter reads every channel in its window, and each filter makes one new channel.

Used in: , , , ,

Source:

Clamping

Holding some units fixed at given values, such as the visible units at a training example, while the rest of the network settles or is sampled around them.

Used in: , ,

Source:

Code

The representation an encoder makes of its input, from which a decoder rebuilds it: usually smaller than the input, or, in a sparse autoencoder, with only a few units active at once.

Used in: , , ,

Source: ; Hinton & Salakhutdinov 2006

Convolution

A small set of weights, a filter, slid across the input, so one pattern is detected wherever it appears.

Each output reads only a few neighbors, which keeps the weights few. Stacked layers see wider and wider regions: in an image, early filters find edges and later ones shapes. WaveNet's dilated convolutions skip inputs, so a few layers reach far back.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Cosine similarity

How closely two vectors point the same way, from 1 (same direction) through 0 (unrelated) to −1 (opposite), whatever their lengths: a common score for comparing embeddings.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Denoiser

The network a diffusion model trains and runs at every step: given a noisy sample and how noisy it is, it predicts the noise (or the clean data), so a little can be taken away.

It is usually a U-Net or a Transformer.

Used in: , ,

Source:

Dilation

Spacing out the inputs a convolution reads, skipping some between each.

Doubling the spacing at each layer lets the reach grow exponentially with depth, so a few layers can see thousands of steps back.

Used in:

Source: ; Yu & Koltun 2015

Edge

A connection between two nodes of a graph.

In a graph network the edges are the input's relations, such as bonds between atoms; in KAN each edge carries its own learned function instead of a single weight.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Encoder and decoder

An encoder turns an input into an internal representation; a decoder turns a representation into an output.

Autoencoders, translation models, and U-Nets pair the two; BERT is an encoder alone and GPT a decoder alone.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Energy

A single number a Hopfield network or Boltzmann machine gives each state of its units, low for states it has learned.

Updates tend to lower it, so the network settles into its stored patterns.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Equilibrium

The state a network of random units settles into after enough updates, where each pattern turns up with a fixed probability that depends on its energy.

Boltzmann machines learn by comparing equilibrium with the data clamped and with it free.

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Feed-forward layer

The small MLP in each Transformer block, applied to every position on its own after attention: it widens each vector, applies an activation function, and narrows it back.

It holds most of a Transformer's parameters, and a mixture of experts replaces it with many.

Used in: , , , , , , , ,

Source:

Filter

A convolution's small set of weights, slid across the input to detect one pattern wherever it appears.

A layer has many filters, each making its own feature map; also called a kernel.

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Gate

A number between 0 and 1, computed from the input, that scales a signal: near 0 shuts it out, near 1 lets it through.

LSTMs and GRUs use gates to decide what their state keeps, forgets, and shows; Mamba's selective state works the same way. The guide draws a gate as a dotted line ending at a dot on the arrow it acts on.

Used in: , , , , ,

Source:

Gaussian bump

A bell-shaped response: largest at a center point and falling off smoothly with distance from it.

Each unit of a radial basis network responds this way to inputs near its center.

Used in:

Source:

Graph

A set of nodes joined by edges, such as atoms and bonds, people and friendships, or roads and junctions.

A graph network works on it directly, so it handles any number of nodes in any arrangement.

Used in:

Source:

Head

A small output layer on a shared network, turning its features into one answer: a class, the probability of each action, a value.

In attention, a head is one of several attention steps run side by side, each with its own queries, keys, and values, so each can look for something different.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source:

Invertible

Able to be run backward exactly: every output comes from one input, which can be recovered.

A normalizing flow is built from invertible layers chosen so that their effect on probability is cheap to compute, which is what makes its likelihood exact.

Used in:

Source:

Kernel

A function scoring how alike two inputs are, such as a Gaussian bump of the distance between them.

Kernel methods such as support vector machines work entirely through such scores; each unit of a radial basis network is one kernel, measured against its center. (A convolution's filter is also called its kernel.)

Used in: ,

Source: ; Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Latent

Hidden.

A latent vector is the compact code a network computes or samples rather than sees: what an autoencoder squeezes its input into, or the space a VAE or GAN draws from to make something new.

Used in: , , , ,

Source:

Masking

Hiding part of what a network may see: tokens swapped for a mask token for it to fill in (BERT, masked diffusion LLMs), or positions attention may not read (a causal mask).

Used in: , ,

Source: ;

Message passing

How a graph network updates each node: every neighbor sends it a message computed from its own state, and the node combines them with its state.

Repeating it lets information travel one edge farther each round.

Used in:

Source: ;

Mixture of experts

A layer made of many expert networks, of which a router picks a few for each token, so the model holds far more parameters than any one token runs through.

It can grow without costing proportionally more to run, and many of today's largest language models use it. The Routing entry steps through it.

Used in:

Source: Jacobs et al. 1991;

Node

A point in a graph, such as an atom or a person, joined to others by edges.

In a graph network each node holds a vector, updated from its neighbors' messages; in KAN a node just adds up what its edges bring.

Used in: ,

Source:

Normalization

Rescaling a layer's numbers to a standard spread, so signals stay in a steady range as they pass through many layers and training stays stable.

Layer normalization works on each token's vector, batch normalization on each feature across a batch.

Used in: Most deep networks since 2015, and every Transformer block.

Source: Ioffe & Szegedy 2015; Ba, Kiros & Hinton 2016

Pooling

Shrinking a feature map by summarizing each small patch, usually by its largest value.

It keeps whether a pattern appeared while forgetting exactly where, and lets later layers see more of the input for the same cost.

Used in:

Source: ; Riesenhuber & Poggio 1999

Position

A slot in a sequence: one token, one time step, or one patch.

Attention on its own ignores order, so Transformers add positional encodings: the original added a fixed pattern of waves to each token's vector, BERT and ViT learn one per position, and most recent language models rotate queries and keys by their position instead (RoPE).

Used in: , , , , ,

Source: ; Su et al. 2021

Prior

The distribution a generative model draws its codes or noise from before generating, usually a plain Gaussian.

A VAE is trained to keep its codes close to it, so any code drawn from the prior decodes to something plausible.

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Query, key, and value

The three vectors attention makes from each position, each by its own learned weights.

A position's query is compared with every key; the better the match, the more of that position's value it takes, like a lookup that returns a blend instead of one entry.

Used in: , , , , , , , ,

Source:

Read and write heads

The parts of a memory-augmented network that read from and write to its memory.

Each produces soft weights over the memory's rows, by content or by location, so reading and writing are differentiable and can be trained by backpropagation.

Used in:

Source:

Recurrence

Running the same network once per step of a sequence, passing a state from each step to the next: a running summary of everything so far.

The state is what lets the network remember, and squeezing all of history into it is what makes long memories hard.

Used in: , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Reparameterization trick

Writing a random sample as the network's outputs plus independent noise, a mean plus a spread times a standard random number, so the error can be passed back through the sampling step.

It is what lets a VAE train by backpropagation.

Used in:

Source:

Residual connection

A path that carries a layer's input around it and adds it to the layer's output, so the layer only has to learn a change.

It lets very deep networks train, because the signal, and in training its gradient, can pass straight through. Also called a skip connection; U-Net's skip connections copy instead of adding.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , , ,

Source:

Residual stream

The running vector that residual connections carry through a deep network: each block reads it and adds its own output back, so the stream builds up every block's contribution.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Routing

Sending each input to only some of a network's parts.

In a mixture of experts a router scores the experts for each token and picks a few, so the network can be large while each token runs through a small part of it. CapsNet's routing by agreement instead sends each capsule's output to the higher capsules that agree with it.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Solver

A numerical method that follows a velocity forward in small steps, as for an ordinary differential equation (ODE).

Flow-matching and diffusion models sample this way; better solvers take bigger steps with little loss in quality.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Spline

A smooth curve made of short polynomial pieces joined end to end, shaped by a few control values.

The original KAN learns one spline per edge; later versions swap in other curves that run faster.

Used in:

Source:

State space model

A recurrence built from linear updates of a hidden state, an idea from control theory.

Because each update is linear, training can compute a whole sequence in parallel, while generating runs one step at a time with a state of fixed size. Mamba makes the updates depend on the input (selective), so it can choose what to keep.

Used in: ,

Source: Gu, Goel & Ré 2021;

Velocity

The direction and speed a point should move at a given moment, as a vector.

Flow matching trains its network to output it, and sampling follows it step by step; the guide marks it with an arrow.

Used in:

Source:

Window

The few neighboring positions an operation reads at once, such as a convolution's three inputs.

Sliding it along the input applies the same operation everywhere; a wider or dilated window reaches farther with no extra weights.

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Objectives

Adversarial training

Training two networks against each other: a generator makes fakes, and a discriminator tries to tell them from real data.

Each improves by beating the other, until the fakes are hard to tell apart.

Used in:

Source:

Competitive learning

Units compete for each input: the one whose weights match it best wins and moves its weights toward it, and in a Kohonen map so do its neighbors on the map.

Over many inputs each unit comes to stand for one kind of input.

Used in:

Source: ; Rumelhart & Zipser 1985

Contrastive learning

Training embeddings by pulling matching pairs together and pushing mismatched ones apart, such as a photo and its caption against the other captions in the batch.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Hebbian learning

Strengthening the weight between two units that are active together, often summed up as cells that fire together wire together.

A Hopfield network stores its patterns this way, in one pass, with no error passed back.

Used in:

Source: Hebb 1949;

Likelihood

How probable a model finds some data.

Training to raise it teaches the model to assign high probability to real examples; a normalizing flow computes it exactly, a VAE a lower bound on it.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016;

Masked-token prediction

Training a model to fill in tokens hidden from it (BERT hides 15%), using the tokens on both sides.

It suits a model that reads the whole text at once; a masked diffusion LLM generates by repeating it, unmasking a few tokens at a time.

Used in: ,

Source:

Next-token prediction

Training a model to predict each token from the ones before it, so ordinary text supplies its own answers.

It is how GPT-style language models learn; to generate, the model predicts a token, adds it to the text, and predicts again.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Bengio et al. 2003;

Noise and denoising

Noise is random variation, here added on purpose.

A denoising model learns to remove it; a diffusion model learns to remove it a little at a time, so it can start from pure noise and end with new data. A GAN's generator turns noise into data in one pass.

Used in: , , , , ,

Source: ;

Reconstruction

Training a network to reproduce its own input, usually through a narrow middle, so it must learn what matters about the data to get it back.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ; Hinton & Salakhutdinov 2006

Variational bound

A lower bound on how probable a model with a hidden code finds the data, trained in place of that probability, which can't be computed exactly.

A VAE's bound rewards rebuilding the input while keeping its codes close to a simple prior, so a code drawn from the prior decodes to something new. Diffusion models train on a simplified form of the same bound.

Used in: ,

Source:

Training

Backpropagation

How a network finds which way to change each weight.

It passes the error back from the output, layer by layer, giving each weight its share of the blame, its gradient; gradient descent then moves every weight a small step the other way. Repeated over many examples, this is what training means for most networks here.

Used in: Nearly every network here; not the Hopfield network, the Boltzmann machines, or the Kohonen map, which learn by local rules.

Source:

Contrastive divergence

A fast way to train an RBM: start Gibbs sampling at the data, run only a step or a few, and nudge the weights toward the data and away from the short run's result.

It approximates maximum-likelihood training without waiting for equilibrium. Not related to contrastive learning.

Used in: ,

Source:

Distillation

Training a model, the student, to reproduce another's outputs, the teacher's: to make a smaller or faster copy.

For diffusion and flow models it cuts sampling from many steps to a few.

Used in: ,

Source: Hinton, Vinyals & Dean 2015

Fine-tuning

Training a pretrained model a little further, on a smaller dataset for a specific task, starting from its learned weights rather than from scratch.

It is far cheaper than pretraining and adapts the model's features to the task.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Gibbs sampling

Sampling from a network of random units by updating some of them, each drawn given the rest, over and over.

Run long enough it reaches equilibrium; in an RBM a whole layer can be drawn at once, since its units don't connect to each other.

Used in: , ,

Source: Geman & Geman 1984;

Loss

A number that measures how far a network's output is from what it should be; training lowers it.

Each panel's objective says what its loss rewards.

Used in: Nearly every network here; not the Hopfield network or the Kohonen map, which follow update rules instead.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Post-training

The training a pretrained language model gets before release: fine-tuning on examples of good answers, then reinforcement learning, such as RLHF, toward answers people prefer.

It turns a text predictor into an assistant.

Used in: ,

Source:

Pre-training

Training a model first on a large, general task, such as predicting words across much of the web, so it learns broadly useful features before any specific use.

A DBN pretrains one layer at a time; BERT and GPT pretrain on text.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Sampling

Drawing an output at random from a model's probabilities instead of always taking the likeliest one, which is how generative models give varied results.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Self-supervised learning

Training on answers the data supplies itself: hide part of the input, or the next word, and ask the network for it.

It needs no labels, so it can learn from vast amounts of text and images; it is how today's language models are pretrained.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Supervised learning

Training on inputs paired with answers that people provided, such as photos labeled with what they show.

The network is corrected toward each answer, its target. Most classifiers here, from the perceptron to ResNet, learn this way.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Training and inference

Training adjusts a model's weights from data; inference runs the finished model on new inputs, with its weights fixed.

Training happens once, at great cost; inference happens every time the model is used, so its cost per input matters most once a model is in use.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Unsupervised learning

Training with no answers at all: the network finds structure in the data on its own, such as clusters, compact codes, or the data's overall shape.

The Kohonen map, Boltzmann machines, and autoencoders learn this way.

Used in: , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ; Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016

Vanishing gradient

The error passed back through many layers, or many steps of a recurrence, shrinking a little at each until the earliest weights barely learn.

It long made deep and recurrent networks hard to train; LSTM gates, residual connections, ReLU activations, and careful starting weights all answer it.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: Hochreiter 1991; Bengio, Simard & Frasconi 1994

Reinforcement learning

Action

What an agent does at each step, chosen by its policy: push left or right, move a piece, write a token.

The environment responds with a new state and a reward.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018

Actor and critic

The two parts of an actor-critic method.

The actor is the policy, choosing actions; the critic estimates the value of a state, the total reward still expected from it (the return). Comparing what happened with the critic's estimate tells the actor which actions did better than expected.

Used in:

Source: ; Sutton & Barto 2018

Clipping

Capping how far one training step may move the policy: PPO stops rewarding a change once an action's probability has moved more than about 20% from before the step.

It keeps learning steady, since one lucky or unlucky batch can't swing the policy far.

Used in:

Source:

Environment

Everything outside the network that it acts on: a game, a simulator, a robot's surroundings, a person rating answers.

It takes each action and returns the next state and a reward. The guide draws it as an outlined box.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018

Policy

In reinforcement learning, the network that chooses actions: given the current state, it gives the probability of each action, and one is drawn.

Policy-gradient methods train it directly, making well-rewarded actions more likely.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018;

Reinforcement learning

Learning by trial and error.

A network, the policy, chooses actions, and the environment returns rewards: scores for how well things went. Training makes actions that led to more reward more likely. RLHF fine-tunes language models this way, with rewards from a model trained on people's preferences.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018;

Reward

The score the environment returns after an action, such as +1 for each step the pole stays up.

Training aims for the most reward over time, not at each step; in RLHF a model trained on people's preferences gives it.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018;

Model families

Autoregressive model

A model that generates one piece at a time, each predicted from everything before it, feeding each output back in as the next input.

Most language models work this way; diffusion language models fill in many tokens at once instead.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Diffusion

Generating data by learning to undo a gradual noising: a network is trained to remove a little noise at a time, then run from pure noise, step by step, to make something new.

The Diffusion model panel draws it; masked diffusion LLMs do the same with masked tokens.

Used in: , , ,

Source: ;

Generator and discriminator

The two networks of a GAN.

The generator turns random noise into a sample; the discriminator sees real data and the generator's samples and guesses which is which. After training, only the generator is kept.

Used in:

Source:

Normalizing flow

A generative model built from invertible steps that turn simple noise into data and back, so it can say exactly how probable any data is.

Flow matching trains a continuous one, whose steps are tiny moves along a learned velocity.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Tasks and data

Clustering

Grouping data points that lie close together, with no labels.

A radial basis network often places its centers by clustering the training data, and a Kohonen map clusters as it learns.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Principal component

A direction along which data varies most; the first few give the best straight-line compression of the data.

A linear autoencoder with a narrow middle learns the same subspace, so it takes nonlinear layers to do better.

Used in:

Source:

Quantization

Rounding values to one of a fixed set of levels.

WaveNet quantizes each audio sample to one of 256 values, so it can predict the next as a choice among them with a softmax. (Quantizing a model's weights to fewer bits, to save memory, is the same idea.)

Used in:

Source:

Segmentation

Labeling every pixel of an image with what it shows, such as cell or background, rather than labeling the image as a whole.

A U-Net outputs a full-size map for it.

Used in:

Source:

Zero-shot

Doing a task with no training examples of it.

CLIP classifies an image by comparing it with captions such as “a photo of a dog”, so it can use labels it was never trained on.

Used in: ,

Source:

Scale

Context window

How many tokens a model can take into account at once: its working memory.

Attention's cost grows with it, which is why linear-time and hybrid models aim at long contexts.

Used in: , , , , ,

Source:

KV cache

The keys and values a Transformer keeps for every earlier token as it generates, so each new token can attend to them without recomputing them.

It grows with the context, and so does the cost of each new token; recurrent and state-space layers keep a fixed-size state instead.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ; Pope et al. 2022

Quadratic and linear time

Attention compares every pair of positions, so its work grows with the square of the length: twice the text, four times the work.

Recurrent and state-space models carry a fixed-size state instead, so their work grows only in step with the length.

Used in: , , , , ,

Source:
